We’re writing to share that you’ll see a new type of block in the code editor today. Meet the Network Connectivity block, which you can find in the Sensing menu.



Over the years, some Scratchers have created projects that check the user’s online status by adapting existing blocks/extensions. The Network Connectivity block will allow your project to check whether or not a user is online easily – no workarounds required.

We hope you enjoy creating with this block! If you’re curious about how it works, read our Q&A below to learn more.

Scratch On!
The Scratch Team

Q&A

How does the Network Connectivity block work?
This block only runs on your own device, and is not storing any data about you. When a user plays a project with the Network Connectivity block, it runs a check back to your browser to see whether the browser believes your device is currently connected to the internet. The information it returns is a simple “yes” or “no.”

Why did you release this block?
Some Scratchers adapt existing blocks/extensions to check whether or not users are online. This block provides a built-in solution to Scratchers who want to include this function in their projects.

Can I use the Network Connectivity block to see if (my friend/my favorite Scratcher/the Scratch Team) is online?
No – this block can’t return information about any other Scratchers. Network Connectivity blocks are connecting back to your browser only as you run a project that uses them. The information about whether or not you’re online is only visible to you.

Hey there –

We want to address some of your concerns about the new Terms of Service .

We use aggregated and anonymized data to better understand what is working about Scratch (and what is not), not to gather any information about any individual. The information Scratch collects will not include names or personal details, and it isn’t–and won’t be–used to identify individual Scratchers.

Having a view of the community’s experience as a whole helps us make the community and platform better for you: whether you’re brand new or you’ve been making projects for years. Guiding Stars
Our “Guiding Stars” shape the design of AI features:

Creativity: Empower kids’ self-expression
Agency: Keep power and choice in kids’ hands
Equity: Make it free, fair, inclusive, and accessible
Community: Emphasize human connection and collaboration

Lines in the Sand
Our “Lines in the Sand” are boundaries we set for the responsible use of AI in Scratch:

Safe: Prevent harmful content
Ethical: Protect children’s data
Transparent: Share information about how it works
Human-Centered: Never undermine human agency or relationships

We also want to assure you that right now, we are not training any AI models on Scratchers’ data. Our work in this space is still in progress and as we iterate and improve our approach to AI, we want to hear from you. We will create opportunities to invite our community to test and provide feedback on AI-powered features as we design them, and you are always invited to send your thoughts to us; we read every message, and we are listening. Like everything at Scratch, we’re building these new features with you in mind, and doing our best to keep Scratch a safe, fun place for you to create what you imagine.

We’re looking forward to sharing more with you soon.

Hey, Scratchers!

As you’ve likely seen, we rolled out new Terms of Service today. We want to share more about what these updates mean for you and for Scratch.

Parental Consent

In order to comply with laws and regulations in your local area, we’ve made some changes to how parental permission works on Scratch. If you are under the legal age required to consent to use Scratch in your state/country, you’ll need to get permission from a parent or guardian to continue using Scratch. Whenever we ask you to agree to something, like changes to our Terms of Service, you’ll need to review that with a parent, too. This change is to ensure your safety and the safety of the entire Scratch community.

Using Data to Improve Scratch

With tens of millions of Scratchers around the world, Scratch has grown into a global community where kids like you express themselves, explore ideas, and build friendships through creative coding. We’re now exploring new AI-powered tools designed to support this community with even more ways of creating.

The tools we’re imagining will help you with things like exploring ideas, understanding code, or getting unstuck – not to do the creating for you. Your imagination, decisions, and voice will always come first. You can learn more about our approach to AI here .

When people use Scratch, we learn from what they create and how they explore the site. This helps us understand what’s working well and what we can improve. Occasionally, we may share anonymized and aggregated information with trusted partners to help us discover what helps you use Scratch better. We’ll use this information to do things like improve project discovery, make onboarding into the community clearer and easier, and improve experiences and features across Scratch for everyone.

This information will not include names or personal details, and it isn’t–and cannot be–used to identify individual Scratchers.

We’re committed to being thoughtful and transparent as we make these changes. Thanks for being part of the Scratch community.

Calling all youth leaders on Scratch!

Applications are officially open for our new Scratch Mentor Program for Scratch, a program within the Scratch Youth Leadership Lab. This program builds on programs already in existence such as the Scratch Design Studio and Scratch Special Events. Members of the Scratch Mentor Program will have opportunities to design and manage studios, act as a role model and resource for others in the community, lead and guide volunteers during programming activities, and help shape Scratch’s big events throughout the year.

Applications open today, January 7 and close on February 1 (at 11:59PM EST).

Everyone interested is encouraged to apply and you can do so here.

To learn more about the application process, see the FAQ below.

We are looking forward to getting started with this exciting new program!
- ceebee, on behalf of the Scratch Team

FAQ

What is the Youth Leadership Lab?
The Youth Leadership Lab is a program at Scratch that aims to provide opportunities for young people to engage in leadership roles and contribute positively to the Scratch community. The Leadership Lab consists of unique tiers, each building off the previous one and providing new opportunities for young people to get involved in the community and develop valuable skills. The Youth Advisory Board, launched in July 2024, is one of these tiers and the Scratch Mentor Program, launched in June 2025, is another one of these tiers.

What is the Scratch Mentor Program?
The Scratch Mentor Program, a program within the Youth Leadership Lab, builds on programs already in existence such as the Scratch Design Studio and Scratch Special Events. Members of the Scratch Mentor Program will have opportunities to design and manage studios, act as a role model and resource for others in the community, lead and guide volunteers during programming activities, and help shape Scratch’s big events throughout the year.

Is this program for me?
Yes! We are looking for Scratchers who are interested in leadership opportunities within Scratch. This could include Scratchers who have already participated in leadership programs like the Welcoming Committee, Scratch Design Studio, Front Page Curator, Scratch Camp Counselor, etc. It could also include Scratchers who have created and led their own studios within Scratch, Scratchers who are interested in expanding their leadership role in the community, and/or are eager to deepen their engagement with the platform and expand their skills. If any of this sounds like you, then we encourage you to apply!

Is there an age requirement?
All Scratchers under the age of 18 who are interested in the program are encouraged to apply.

How long does someone serve on the Scratch Mentor Program?
Currently, we are asking for a 6 month commitment.

How much of a time commitment is this program?
This will vary a bit depending on what aspects of the program are happening but generally, there will be opportunities to participate every month. This is a voluntary position in which you are free to participate as much or as little as you would like.

How many people will be accepted?
We will accept up to 50 applicants.

What about Scratchers who are already in the Mentor Program?
Scratchers who are already in the Mentor Program are automatically invited to continue with the program (if they are interested in doing so) as we recognize their previous involvements and want to continue our collaborations with them!

I live in a different country or time zone than the Scratch Team. Can I still apply?
Yes, definitely! The Scratch community is a global community and we want to make sure this is reflected in the Scratch Mentor Program.

How do I apply?
The application is done in two parts. The first part is an online form and the second part is the creation of a Scratch project that addresses specific questions. We will also need to chat with a parent or legal guardian as part of the process to make sure you have their permission to participate in the program. See all the details here .

When is the application deadline?
All applications must be submitted by the end of the day on February 1, 2026 (no later than 11:59PM EST).

I’ve applied. Now what?
Once the application process is closed, we will review all of the applications to determine who will be invited to join the Scratch Mentor Program. We will let everyone know individually by email if your application was accepted or not. Please keep in mind it will take us some time to review everything so it may take a few weeks for us to get back to you! We will send emails to everyone on the same day.

I applied but wasn’t accepted. What else can I participate in?
There are lots of ways to participate in leadership opportunities on Scratch! Being friendly and welcome to others on Scratch, providing constructive feedback on projects, and hosting your own studios are all wonderful ways to show leadership on Scratch! We also have a few specific spaces you can check out right away that are always looking for additional helpers. This includes the Scratch Design Studio (always featured on the 4th row of the Scratch homepage ), the Welcoming Committee , and the Front Page Curator program . We can’t wait to see what you will do ^.^

FAQ

Is Face Sensing safe and private?
Yes. The images from your webcam are never transmitted outside of your device. Face Sensing blocks detect faces using a technology called “machine learning” (a subset of AI that enables machines to learn from data), but it is not training on your data while you use it. It has already been trained to see faces using a large number of photos of faces.

Was Face Sensing tested in Scratch Lab?
Yes! You may remember Face Sensing blocks from Scratch Lab, the space for the Scratch Team to test experimental blocks. Your feedback in Scratch Lab helped us improve the way these blocks work before this new feature was ready for release—thank you!

I made a Face Sensing project in Scratch Lab. Can I share it on Scratch?
Yes! You can upload and share any Scratch Lab projects you’ve created using Face Sensing blocks. As soon as these blocks are live (update: they are live now!), your Scratch project will work the same as it does in Scratch Lab. Just choose File>Load from My Computer in the project editor.

If I use the “Set Thumbnail” button while my face is on-screen, will it capture an image of my face?
No. When using the Face Sensing extension, none of your data is stored or sent to Scratch or any other site, and your camera view is not captured when setting your project thumbnail, so your data remains private.

What if I want to hide my face/hide the visible video feed without removing the Face Sensing blocks?
Any “Backdrop” created in the Sprite Area on your Face Sensing project will be hidden by default and replaced with your video feed, but you can create backdrops/ backgrounds as sprites instead. If the backdrop sprite covers the entire screen, none of your video feed will be visible, but the program will still be able to “go to nose” or recognize face tilt and face size. You can also use the “set ghost effect” block on the background sprite, if you want your video feed somewhat visible through the backdrop. Or add the Video Sensing Extension and use the “set video transparency block” available there to adjust how visible your video is.

I changed my mind about using Face Sensing blocks in my project, but the video feed is still on my screen. How can I get rid of it?
No problem! If you no longer want to use the Face Sensing extension blocks in your project, remove all of the extension's blocks from the script area (drag blocks to the block palette to delete). Make sure to turn off any stage monitors by ensuring all checkboxes are unchecked in the blocks palette (next to blocks like “face tilt”), too. Save your project. Then, reload the project by refreshing the browser, or closing and reopening the project.

Why don’t Face Sensing blocks see my face?
The technology behind Face Sensing is not perfect. It is best at seeing faces that are brightly lit and close to the camera. It will often recognize faces even if they are partially hidden by a mask, glasses, hat, headscarf, or other covering. It does not do well at seeing faces that are far away, in the dark, or hidden.

Can my action figure/stick figure drawing/plush toy use Face Sensing blocks, too?
Face Sensing blocks can detect faces in photos, and even in drawings. Try holding different things with faces up to your camera and see what happens!

What if my camera is not working?
When you load Face Sensing blocks, you should see video from your webcam on the Scratch stage. If it doesn’t appear, you may need to give Scratch permission to use your camera. Click “allow” when Scratch prompts for permission to use the camera, or check your web browser’s settings.

Does Face Sensing work on all devices?
Our goal is to make Face Sensing blocks work on all devices and web browsers supported by Scratch. Currently, Face Sensing blocks may not work on some Android and iOS devices. They may run slowly on some Chromebooks or older computers.

What can I do if Face Sensing feels slow or laggy?
Face Sensing may run slowly on some devices. You can try closing other applications and browser tabs. If you are using your webcam in another app while Face Sensing is running—for example, a video call—try turning off your camera in that app.

Can I use Face Sensing blocks without a camera?
While you can see and edit the code inside Face Sensing projects without a camera, you’ll need to use your device’s camera in order to use Face Sensing functions.

When will Face Sensing be available in languages other than English?
Scratch’s volunteer translators are working on translating Face Sensing blocks into multiple languages. This work is still in progress, and we hope to share more with you soon.

When will Face Sensing be available offline?
Our team is hard at work making Face Sensing blocks available for downloadable Scratch Apps. We’ll be sure to share an update with you as soon as we have it.

I'm personally already not a fan of the idea of having any kind of biometric data attached to almost anything online, but this is just ridiculous. Nobody needs spy-movie thriller style security systems for their Scratch accounts: last I checked, Scratch isn't a bank, and doesn't have a way of making money off the platform. Although it's not just this ridiculous security concern over Scratch accounts possibly being hacked into, but if we ignore that, there's still many issues with this idea.

  Voice data is quite possibly one of the least private biometrics out there, not to mention one of the easiest to fake. Signatures are thought of as unique, and yet signature forgery has been an almost constant issue for many years simply because they're so easy to fake; voices are very similar to signatures in this way. I'm not sure you've ever heard of voice impression, but it's basically where people replicate a voice, and some people are very good at it, sounding extremely similar to the original actor. But if voice impression is too niche: AI is actually getting scarily good at replicating voices. I get you said that “voice passwords may not sound robotic,” but how do you even detect that? I can quite easily see a comparison tool not being able to tell if a voice sounds robotic, unless you want to suggest throwing AI at this problem (which is a can of worms onto itself).

  Second there is, of course, the issue of implementation. Where is Scratch going to store the data? How would they compare audio clips? What is an appropriate spot on the website to have this be set let alone entered in? How would Scratch make sure that this voice data remains safe and secure? Encryption? Generally in server security only a hash* is kept of the password on the server system, but the issue with that is that even slight deviations in data would result in an entirely different hash, so if they are going to keep a hash, how would they account for details such as background noise that could differ from recording to recording? This simply isn't feasible in any way.

  End note: Hadn't thought about this before but I saw at least a few people bring it up, so I think it's worth at least a note in my post. Remember that Scratch's target age group is very young children, whose voices can change quite a lot as they grow older; in effect, this would lock some people out of their accounts for the crime of aging. Q&A

How does the Network Connectivity block work?
This block only runs on your own device, and is not storing any data about you. When a user plays a project with the Network Connectivity block, it runs a check back to your browser to see whether the browser believes your device is currently connected to the internet. The information it returns is a simple “yes” or “no.”

Why did you release this block?
Some Scratchers adapt existing blocks/extensions to check whether or not users are online. This block provides a built-in solution to Scratchers who want to include this function in their projects.

Can I use the Network Connectivity block to see if (my friend/my favorite Scratcher/the Scratch Team) is online?
No – this block can’t return information about any other Scratchers. Network Connectivity blocks are connecting back to your browser only as you run a project that uses them. The information about whether or not you’re online is only visible to you.

Hey there –

We want to address some of your concerns about the new Terms of Service .

We use aggregated and anonymized data to better understand what is working about Scratch (and what is not), not to gather any information about any individual. The information Scratch collects will not include names or personal details, and it isn’t–and won’t be–used to identify individual Scratchers.

Having a view of the community’s experience as a whole helps us make the community and platform better for you: whether you’re brand new or you’ve been making projects for years. Guiding Stars
Our “Guiding Stars” shape the design of AI features:

Creativity: Empower kids’ self-expression
Agency: Keep power and choice in kids’ hands
Equity: Make it free, fair, inclusive, and accessible
Community: Emphasize human connection and collaboration

Lines in the Sand
Our “Lines in the Sand” are boundaries we set for the responsible use of AI in Scratch:

Safe: Prevent harmful content
Ethical: Protect children’s data
Transparent: Share information about how it works
Human-Centered: Never undermine human agency or relationships

We also want to assure you that right now, we are not training any AI models on Scratchers’ data. Our work in this space is still in progress and as we iterate and improve our approach to AI, we want to hear from you. We will create opportunities to invite our community to test and provide feedback on AI-powered features as we design them, and you are always invited to send your thoughts to us; we read every message, and we are listening. Like everything at Scratch, we’re building these new features with you in mind, and doing our best to keep Scratch a safe, fun place for you to create what you imagine.

Hey, Scratchers!

As you’ve likely seen, we rolled out new Terms of Service today. We want to share more about what these updates mean for you and for Scratch.

Parental Consent

In order to comply with laws and regulations in your local area, we’ve made some changes to how parental permission works on Scratch. If you are under the legal age required to consent to use Scratch in your state/country, you’ll need to get permission from a parent or guardian to continue using Scratch. Whenever we ask you to agree to something, like changes to our Terms of Service, you’ll need to review that with a parent, too. This change is to ensure your safety and the safety of the entire Scratch community.

Using Data to Improve Scratch

With tens of millions of Scratchers around the world, Scratch has grown into a global community where kids like you express themselves, explore ideas, and build friendships through creative coding. We’re now exploring new AI-powered tools designed to support this community with even more ways of creating.

The tools we’re imagining will help you with things like exploring ideas, understanding code, or getting unstuck – not to do the creating for you. Your imagination, decisions, and voice will always come first. You can learn more about our approach to AI here .

When people use Scratch, we learn from what they create and how they explore the site. This helps us understand what’s working well and what we can improve. Occasionally, we may share anonymized and aggregated information with trusted partners to help us discover what helps you use Scratch better. We’ll use this information to do things like improve project discovery, make onboarding into the community clearer and easier, and improve experiences and features across Scratch for everyone.

This information will not include names or personal details, and it isn’t–and cannot be–used to identify individual Scratchers.

We’re committed to being thoughtful and transparent as we make these changes. Thanks for being part of the Scratch community.

What is the Youth Leadership Lab?
The Youth Leadership Lab is a program at Scratch that aims to provide opportunities for young people to engage in leadership roles and contribute positively to the Scratch community. The Leadership Lab consists of unique tiers, each building off the previous one and providing new opportunities for young people to get involved in the community and develop valuable skills. The Scratch Mentor Program, a program within the Youth Leadership Lab, builds on programs already in existence such as the Scratch Design Studio and Scratch Special Events. Is this program for me?
Yes! We are looking for Scratchers who are interested in leadership opportunities within Scratch. This could include Scratchers who have already participated in leadership programs like the Welcoming Committee, Scratch Design Studio, Front Page Curator, Scratch Camp Counselor, etc. It could also include Scratchers who have created and led their own studios within Scratch, Scratchers who are interested in expanding their leadership role in the community, and/or are eager to deepen their engagement with the platform and expand their skills. Is there an age requirement?
All Scratchers under the age of 18 who are interested in the program are encouraged to apply.

How long does someone serve on the Scratch Mentor Program?
Currently, we are asking for a 6 month commitment.

How much of a time commitment is this program?
This will vary a bit depending on what aspects of the program are happening but generally, there will be opportunities to participate every month. This is a voluntary position in which you are free to participate as much or as little as you would like.

How many people will be accepted?
We will accept up to 50 applicants.

What about Scratchers who are already in the Mentor Program?
Scratchers who are already in the Mentor Program are automatically invited to continue with the program (if they are interested in doing so) as we recognize their previous involvements and want to continue our collaborations with them!

Yes, definitely! The Scratch community is a global community and we want to make sure this is reflected in the Scratch Mentor Program.

The application is done in two parts. The first part is an online form and the second part is the creation of a Scratch project that addresses specific questions. When is the application deadline?
All applications must be submitted by the end of the day on February 1, 2026 (no later than 11:59PM EST).

I’ve applied. Now what?
Once the application process is closed, we will review all of the applications to determine who will be invited to join the Scratch Mentor Program. Please keep in mind it will take us some time to review everything so it may take a few weeks for us to get back to you! We will send emails to everyone on the same day.

generally, you want the price to scale faster than the upgrade strength, so for example, if your upgrade doubles cps every time, it should slightly more than double in price, the exact amount depending on what other upgrades you have. This way, the player will quickly hit a wall where the price is much higher than the reward. That should be the point another new upgrade becomes affordable that allows the player to move the wall a bit further until the next thing becomes available.

Another strategy for balancing upgrades is by not having upgrades increase in power at all, this way they quickly become obsolete when bigger upgrades become available, but this method has the drawback that ppls will be spamming upgrades rather than the thing the clicker is about.

Often its a good idea to introduce a new mechanic at the point where the player is familiar with another one and allow the player to (mostly) automate this previous thing. Unnamed Space Idle (a game on Steam) did this very well, allowing it to be engaging even after a year of playing it.

A thumbnail has to accomplish several tasks:
Attract attention,
Pique interest, and
Convince the user to click it.

Attracting attention is primarily done by standing out:
Often bright colours (especially red) attract attention, but in an environment where everything does that, something much more calm would stand out more.

Piquing interest is done by providing the user with enough information to have a vague idea of what the project is about, whilst also making it clear this is not everything.

Convincing the user to click it can finally be done by a combination of the thumbnail and the project name. For this step you want to make the potential user think that it is a project actually worth looking at, for example having a high quality thumbnail suggest the project itself is also high quality. The project name should also be something that sets some high expectations.
